summary: Defines a portion of the Management Information Base for managing user identities and the names, addresses and credentials needed to control access, for use with various IP storage protocols. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: This is a list of gauges and switches a management program can use to see who is allowed to use shared storage, and to change that list.

questions: snmp objects for storage access control
snmp mib for iscsi user identities
how does ips-auth-mib match an identity
subtitle: An SNMP MIB module for listing the users, addresses and credentials allowed to reach IP storage.

tldr.problem: Storage devices that speak protocols such as iSCSI need a standard way to configure and inspect which user identities may access them.
tldr.mechanism: The IPS-AUTH-MIB module defines tables of authorization instances, identities, names, address ranges and credentials. Several rows of one kind are ORed, and different kinds are ANDed.
tldr.outcome: The module only supplies the identities. Other MIB modules point to them with a RowPointer and supply their own access lists.

today: RFC 4545 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2006. The metadata for this unit lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 4545 defines a MIB module, IPS-AUTH-MIB, used to configure or look at the configuration of user identities and their credentials. The motivation was configuring authorized user identities for the iSCSI protocol, but it was extended to suit other protocols with similar needs.

A "user" here need not be a person. It can be a host, an application, a cluster of hosts or any identifiable entity that can be authorized to access a resource. Most objects have a MAX-ACCESS of read-create, and the MIN-ACCESS for all objects is read-only for implementations that configure through other means but need to monitor identities.

The module is written in SMIv2 and accessed through SNMP. It supplies only the set of identities for use in access lists. Other MIB modules must tie them to their own access lists or authorization methods.
sections.eli5: Think of a guest list for a clubhouse. This document defines how a management program can read and edit the guest list, but not who guards the door.

sections.title: Users, SNMPv3 and Contexts
sections.content:
The module does not provide authorization or access control lists. Other modules reference its identities, typically with a RowPointer from a list element to a user identity. It also leaves out login and authentication failure statistics and notifications as too application specific, so no notifications are provided or required.

A "user" in this module is a collection of user names, addresses and credentials used together to decide whether to allow access to a resource. Each user can have several of each. That differs from an SNMPv3 user in the User-based Security Model (RFC 3414), which has exactly one user name, one authentication protocol and one privacy protocol. The two are unrelated, though both may live on the same system.

Every non-scalar object is indexed first by an instance, a collection of identities that can authorize access to a resource. Instances do not replace SNMP contexts, but they make it easy to assign a collection of identities to one or more contexts.
sections.eli5: A club member can have several nicknames, several home addresses and several membership cards. This module lets all of those be written down under one member.

sections.title: The Object Model
sections.content:
At the top is ipsAuthInstance, a distinct authorization entity in the managed system. Most implementations have just one. Several can be used for a partitioned large system, a set of stackable systems under one agent, or several protocols that each have their own identities.

Inside an instance, ipsAuthIdentity is a user identity. It holds only a description. Its names, addresses and credentials sit in their own tables because each can have many values.

The matching rule is simple. Several rows of one type are treated as OR, and an entity need match only one. Rows of different types are treated as AND, so an entity must match at least one row from each category. A category with no rows is ignored. For example, with two address rows, one credential row and no name rows, an entity must match the credential and at least one of the addresses.

Index values are referenced in several tables, so an implementation should keep them persistent across reboots, and indexes of deleted rows must not be reused before a reboot.
sections.eli5: To get in, you need to match one item from each non-empty pile: your name, where you live, or your card. If a pile is empty, nobody checks it.

sections.title: Names and Addresses
sections.content:
The name table holds UTF-8 names, each of which may identify the identity. A name is typically unique within its scope and unchanging, and normally meets some or all requirements for a Uniform Resource Name (RFC 1737), though it need not be a URN. An example is the iSCSI Name from RFC 3720. If an identity has no names, no name is checked.

The address table holds ranges at which the identity may reside. Each entry has a start and an end address, and for a single address both must be identical. An address type is an IANA Address Family value, so IPv4, IPv6 or Fibre Channel types are all possible. The address is an octet string. For IPv4 and IPv6 it follows the InetAddress format of RFC 4001, and for Fibre Channel it follows FcNameIdOrZero from RFC 4044.

A match with any range in the list is valid, and an empty list matches any address. Netmasks are not supported because ranges can express the same thing more flexibly.
sections.eli5: A name says who you are. An address range says where you are allowed to be. You can list a single spot by using the same start and end.

sections.title: Credentials and Object Identifiers
sections.content:
Each credential row names an authentication method such as CHAP (RFC 1994), SRP (RFC 2945) or Kerberos (RFC 4120). The method is given as an object identifier rather than an enumerated type, so other MIB modules can add methods without changing this one.

For each credential there is a matching row, with the same indices, in a method-specific table. CHAP and SRP rows hold a user name and Kerberos rows hold a principal. For any other OID, the attributes belong in another module. A new type is added by defining a new OID in the ipsAuthMethodTypes subtree and a new table.

Passwords and verifiers for credentials like CHAP or SRP are managed outside this module.
sections.eli5: A credential is like a type of membership card. Because each card type is labeled by a code, new kinds of cards can be added later without rewriting the rulebook.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Writable objects such as descriptions, row status, storage type, address ranges and credential details can be abused. An attacker could add or delete a rogue identity, widen an allowed address range, or change an authentication method. Removing legitimate credentials can cause denial of service or weaken access requirements. Readable objects are also sensitive, since they reveal which names, addresses and credentials are required for access.

The RFC recommends the SNMPv3 security features, says deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED, and strongly recommends SNMPv3 with a securityLevel of authPriv for all access.

Updates can open windows. If a list is briefly empty, access may be unconstrained, so deleting an old credential before adding the new one must never be done. Safe methods are to write the new value in place, to add the new row and then delete the old, or to do both in one request with the add first. When changing an address range, start and end must be updated in the same set request, or a new row added before the old one is deleted. Changing an address type of an existing row is not allowed.
sections.eli5: The guest list itself is secret and valuable. Change it carefully: never erase the old entry before writing the new one, or for a moment the door is open to everyone.

root.label: ipsAuthInstance
root.note: A distinct authorization entity; most systems have one

items.title: Same type: OR
items.text: Several name, address or credential rows: matching any one is enough.

items.title: Different types: AND
items.text: At least one row from each non-empty category must match.

items.title: Empty category
items.text: A category with no rows is ignored, so anything matches it.
